title: Add test for kernel recovery after unsolicited process death (SIGKILL)
description:
## Context

In posit-dev/positron#13694, we attempted to cover the scenario where a kernel process dies unexpectedly and the supervisor detects and propagates that to the client. Julia's [review comment](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/13694#issuecomment-4512813907) pointed out that the correct layer for this test is Kallichore itself. 

Specifically, test coverage should be against the `run_child` logic in `crates/kcserver/src/kernel_session/process.rs` that calls `child.wait().await` and then sends `WebsocketMessage::Kernel(KernelMessage::Exited(code))` to the client.

The existing `test_kernel_session_shutdown` in `crates/kcserver/tests/python_kernel_tests.rs` covers the graceful shutdown path via `shutdown_request`, but there is no companion test for unsolicited process death.

## Proposed test

A test (e.g., `test_kernel_session_unexpected_death`) in `crates/kcserver/tests/python_kernel_tests.rs` that:

1. Spawns a real Python kernel (using the existing test harness)
2. Captures the kernel PID (e.g., via an `os.getpid()` execute request)
3. Sends SIGKILL to that PID
4. Asserts that a `WebsocketMessage::Kernel(KernelMessage::Exited(_))` event is received over the WebSocket
5. Asserts the session status transitions to the exited state

This would cover the same intent as the Playwright e2e approach but at a fraction of the runtime, with deterministic event-based assertions, and on the layer where a regression would actually originate. It may fit naturally next to `test_kernel_session_shutdown` as its asymmetric counterpart.

## References

- posit-dev/positron#12869: original issue (kernel death over remote SSH)
- posit-dev/positron#13694: Playwright e2e test PR (to be superseded by this)

## Disclaimer and Questions

I'm not very familiar with this repo, so I logged this as a proposal first to see what devs involved with Kallichore think of the approach. It's not urgent, but it'd be great if I could pair up with someone to better understand how the kernel works precisely. 

If you prefer async, please find my main questions below. 

1. What's the most desirable way to get the kernel PID in the test? I see that the sessions list API already exposes `process_id`. Can I just use that, or should I mimic a real client who would execute `os.getpid()` via the kernel?
2. What's the most desireable `exit` code to assert? If I understood correctly, when signal kills the process, then `status.code()` returns `None` and Kallichore maps that to `-1`. I couldn't find other tests asserting `None` or `-1`... should either be preferrable or is just asserting non-zero enough? I'm leaning towards`-1`.
3. Kill during startup vs. kill while idle: Is it ok if the test only covers killing a kernel that's **already running and idle**, or also cover killing it before it finishes starting up? I think the latter is less likely but may also happen, hence why I'm undecided on this. 
4. Since SIGKILL doesn't exist on Windows, would it be ok if coverage is only kept to Unix, and not to Windows?

title: Add an RPC for executing code
description:
Currently, the only way to execute code and get the results is to use the web socket to send a Jupyter `execute_request` and listen for the resulting `iopub` and `execute_reply` messages on the web socket.

However, this requires a websocket library and a bit of boilerplate to filter out all the messages on the stream. 

It would be very helpful for external use (especially with a Quarto engine) to have an RPC usable over regular HTTP that performed an execution and returned the results. 

The RPC's status would mirror that of the execution; it would not return until the execution is finished, and would succeed (200) or fail (non 200) as the execution does. The resultant return value in JSON would aggregate all of the data returned during execution, perhaps as a literal accumulation of all messages from the streams with the same parent ID as the execution, or perhaps as a summary of stdout, stderr, and structured result.

These executions would have the same queuing behaviors (and share a queue with) executions requested via `execute_request`.

title: Don't log error shutting down connections
description:
Due to a recent Axios update, we are now compelled to connect to the Kallichore socket in such a way that kcserver keeps logging these for every RPC made over the domain socket:

```
01:26:29 [DEBUG] (14) kcserver::server: Unix socket connection ended (/var/folders/rh/jyts7h0j3rdgrrqx5xb3phgm0000gp/T/kc-55998.sock): error shutting down connection
01:26:49 [DEBUG] (4) kcserver::server: Unix socket connection ended (/var/folders/rh/jyts7h0j3rdgrrqx5xb3phgm0000gp/T/kc-55998.sock): error shutting down connection
01:27:09 [DEBUG] (14) kcserver::server: Unix socket connection ended (/var/folders/rh/jyts7h0j3rdgrrqx5xb3phgm0000gp/T/kc-55998.sock): error shutting down connection
01:27:29 [DEBUG] (14) kcserver::server: Unix socket connection ended (/var/folders/rh/jyts7h0j3rdgrrqx5xb3phgm0000gp/T/kc-55998.sock): error shutting down connection
01:27:49 [DEBUG] (4) kcserver::server: Unix socket connection ended (/var/folders/rh/jyts7h0j3rdgrrqx5xb3phgm0000gp/T/kc-55998.sock): error shutting down connection
01:28:09 [DEBUG] (14) kcserver::server: Unix socket connection ended (/var/folders/rh/jyts7h0j3rdgrrqx5xb3phgm0000gp/T/kc-55998.sock): error shutting down connection
```

This is noisy, and not actually a problem due to the way Axios handles the socket connection upstream, so we should stop logging this altogether to avoid people fixating on it as a possible issue when analyzing logs.

title: Don't use portpicker
description:
The portpicker crate has been observed to cause various problems:
- it requires the port to be free on TCP and UDP
- using it guarantees a race condition since some time must elapse between the time portpicker says "this port is free" and the time you try to use the port
- we have seen at least one case in the wild wherein it literally cannot find a free port despite other networking on the machine appearing to be fine

@DavisVaughan outlined a mechanism we could use to remove our dependency on portpicker:

If you can make it work, I'd be in favor of dropping portpicker from this process altogether.

When you do the port stuff here:

https://github.com/posit-dev/kallichore/blob/cdec434f2f620545bfe47004300f41e60d0bd45b/crates/kcserver/src/main.rs#L155-L178

What if you instead went ahead and created a TcpListener with bind() that immediately binds to either a user provided or OS provided port?

https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/net/struct.TcpListener.html#method.bind

You can get the selected port back out with the port() method on the return value of this:

https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/net/struct.TcpListener.html#method.local_addr

And you can write that to the connection file

Then you'd pass the TcpListener through to server::create() instead of just the address, and you'd use Server::from_tcp() rather than 
Server::bind() here

https://github.com/posit-dev/kallichore/blob/cdec434f2f620545bfe47004300f41e60d0bd45b/crates/kcserver/src/server.rs#L108

That avoids:
- Any weirdness from portpicker, instead relying on battle tested std::net::TcpListener::bind() code for picking the port
- Any chance UDP could have been the problem
- Any chance of a race condition between when portpicker picked the free port, and when you actually bind to it in server::create(), which does currently exist

title: Registration socket should bind to port `0` for JEP 66
description:
Test failure on Positron
https://d38p2avprg8il3.cloudfront.net/playwright-report-14311774413-14996/index.html#?testId=427ee434beaa61d48e51-a4047b27dffbed252249

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6486592f-2520-412f-8fd2-51050766ebb2)

Kallichore picks the registration port here but does not bind to it
https://github.com/posit-dev/kallichore/blob/68dbcee01e34aa928e2ebf53d90e7c487f236ce5/crates/kcserver/src/kernel_session.rs#L156-L165

Instead it binds to it a little bit later on, here:
https://github.com/posit-dev/kallichore/blob/68dbcee01e34aa928e2ebf53d90e7c487f236ce5/crates/kcserver/src/registration_socket.rs#L179-L180

The gap of time between picked port and bound port can result in the error you see in the picture where some other process has connected to that port in the meantime.

The solution for kallichore is probably the same solution we use in ark. Pass `0` as the port to `bind()` against. This lets the OS pick the port (and seems to work on all OSes) and immediately bind to it, avoiding any race condition. There _should_ be a way to then extract the port from the zeromq `RepSocket` after it has been created, and if there is not we should ask them for that feature upstream, because using port `0` in this way is a very common thing to do.

title: Add a non-Websocket API to execute code and return results
description:
If you want to execute code using Kallichore today, you must first open a websocket and then send Jupyter messages through the socket. That's okay for Positron where streaming output is very important, but is a less convenient API for other consumers that just want to run code and get results. 

An example might be having Kallichore run code on behalf of an LLM; it would be easier to hook up the LLM to a code execution endpoint than try to have it wrangle a websocket connection (esp. if Positron is already connected; currently only one socket at a time can be connected to a session).

We could add a code execution API that just takes the code to execute and returns the results, for easy integration with other tools.

title: Add a 'nudge' endpoint or equivalent to extend idle timeout
description:
Right now the idle timeout can expire _while Positron is still connected_, in the case where the supervisor isn't running any sessions yet. For example this can happen:

- user opens a new workspace but doesn't start any sessions
- user leaves workspace running for a couple of hours, idle
- Kallichore shuts down due to inactivity (no sessions running for over an hour, nothing connected)
- user finally tries to start a session
- fails because server isn't running any more

Probably rare but needs to be defended against. Unlike the websocket connections, the connection to Positron itself isn't stateful, so we need some kind of polling to see if it's still going.

Proposal:

- add a new API that nudges the idle timeout
- have Positron call this API in some interval that is ~1/2 the idle timeout, e.g. every 30 minutes

title: When supervisor is set to run indefinitely, have it (optionally?) shut down after all sessions have exited
description:
Currently, if you run Kallichore without an idle timeout, it will run forever. This might not be desirable in some configurations. For example, on Positron Desktop, once you configure the supervisor to let kernels run indefinitely, you can no longer get rid of the supervisor process without some sort of drastic action (running the 'restart kernel supervisor' command, reboot, etc.).

If Kallichore is started without an idle timeout, it should still exit by default if it isn't running anything. In some configurations (e.g. running a remote server) it might be better to let it run -- we could add a command line option for this? --- but in most cases exiting is preferable.

title: Allocate sockets on kernel start, not kernel create
description:
Currently, Kallichore allocates the ZeroMQ sockets when a new kernel session is created. The sockets remain allocated (but not bound) until the session is later started.

This is is a contributor to the startup race condition for socket allocation. We should not allocate sockets until _just_ before they are used, to minimize the time between allocation and binding. That means moving socket allocation from the create API to the start API.

(Could be done in combination with https://github.com/posit-dev/kallichore/issues/2)

title: Add a heartbeat check, websocket, or endpoint
description:
While individual kernels have heartbeats, Kallichore itself doesn't. This can make it difficult for clients to be notified if the server process goes down. 

Kallichore should have a simple RPC that can be called for health checks, and/or SSE or websockets for detecting offline status quickly.

title: Reject (or handle graciously) session IDs that aren't URL safe
description:
There are no restrictions on session IDs in Kallichore; you can make one that's zero length or has unprintable or unusual Unicode characters. This can make it difficult to invoke API methods on those sessions since the session ID is read from the URL.

There are a few ways to address this; the simplest is probably to require session IDs to use characters from a limited URL-safe set, have a min and max length, etc.

title: Crash recovery: a supervisor crash could be survivable
description:
Currently, a crash in the supervisor also takes down every single kernel. This is undesirable since it could cause a lot of work to be lost and a panic in the supervisor is always possible.

- Run the kernels such that they are either children of some other parent process, or figure out a way to run them as child processes that get re-parented when Kallichore exits instead of getting killed themselves.
- Store the metadata about active kernels -- their 0MQ socket ports, HMAC keys, names, etc. -- in someplace durable (e.g. a JSON file or a sqlite3 database) while running. This can serve as a crash recovery database.
- When starting up, read the crash recovery database if it exists, and try to reconnect to the kernels.

Related to #3.

title: Remove "KS-nnn" from error messages in API responses
description: Error messages sent from Kallichore as API responses currently have a text representation of the error message that includes the error code (`KS-nnn`). They shouldn't since the API already sends the error code as a separate field and the UI may not want to show the code twice (or show it at all).

title: Add arm64 builds for Linux
description: Kallichore currently only has x64 Linux builds. To support all Workbench platforms (as well as arm64 versions of Remote SSH sessions in Positron), it should also have arm64 Linux builds.

title: Do not enter kernel ready state until after kernel info reply
description:
Currently, Kallichore enters the kernel Ready state as soon as it gets a heartbeat from the kernel. This is overly optimistic; Positron's Jupyter Adapter has a more pessimistic behavior wherein it uses kernel info requests to probe the kernel for readiness, which is a more reliable way to see whether the kernel is actually open for business. Details here:

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/pull/2207

Positron always sends a kernel info request when it starts the kernel. If we are sending a request from Kallichore internally too, that feels a little sloppy. Some possible resolutions:
- the "Start Kernel" API could resolve with the kernel info request's payload, so that Positron doesn't have to send another request to get the data
- we could cache the kernel's response for a short period of time so that we don't have to ask for it again
- we could just live with two requests, it's not that bad

We could also use the initial kernel info request to populate the initial input/continuation prompt fields (see #10).

Also note that _some_ kernels support a way to detect a ready state on IOPub. We can't rely on this, though, so we need the above scheme for kernels that don't (pretty much all of them right now?). See #1.

title: Track input prompt and continuation prompt in each kernel
description:
As in #9, we need to track the input prompt and continuation prompt as they change, so that these fields are correct in the API. 

Note that these prompts are returned in the kernel info request, as a Posit extension to the Jupyter protocol nested in the language information.

https://github.com/posit-dev/ark/blob/ba2bf26debd055e84c1bb61171dd956be06959f0/crates/ark/src/shell.rs#L166-L169

Also as in the working directory issue, we need to decide whether to pick these up by spying or doing some sort of direct interrogation.

title: Track current working directory in each kernel
description:
Kallichore currently reports the current working directory of the kernel via the API, but that information is wrong if the working directory has changed since the kernel was started.

There are a few ways we could try to fix this:

- try to get the working directory from the process itself using system APIs
- spy on the messages on the UI comm that are sent to Positron to update its UI
- ask the kernel what its working directory is by using the UI comm ourselves or via some other dedicated means

title: Add API to adopt an already-running kernel
description:
Positron's Reticulate support works by starting up an ipykernel instance inside R instead of asking the Jupyter Adapter to set it up. Then, it tells the Jupyter kernel wrapper to connect to the session.

https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/e8329ddd02c36358d9f38d50f46e0d88150fa5ee/extensions/positron-python/src/client/jupyter-adapter.d.ts#L11-L35

This workflow is not compatible with Kallichore since -- currently -- Kallichore only connects to sessions it starts itself.

Kallichore should have an API method that does the equivalent of `connectToSession` above; that is, it connects to an already-running session, but other than not starting (or owning) the session process, it treats that session like any other, connects to its 0MQ sockets, provides a Websocket proxy, etc.

title: Support for a binary Websocket protocol
description:
Kallichore's Websocket protocol is modeled after that of the [Jupyter kernel gateway](https://jupyter-kernel-gateway.readthedocs.io/en/latest/websocket-mode.html#websocket-resources); that is, it sends text messages over the websocket that are well-formed JSON.

```json
{
    "channel": "iopub",
    "header": {
        "msg_type": "example"
    },
    "content": {
        "example": true
    }
}
```

This text-based representation has a few upsides:

- it makes debugging a lot easier since you can examine the message and its contents as simple strings
- it makes it easier to compose valid socket messages using high-level tools and in test frameworks

However, it also has a few downsides:

- it is not very space efficient
- it is unfriendly to raw binary data such as the message buffers (which we are currently base64 encoding)
- it is slightly more computationally expensive since everything needs to be serialized on the backend and then parsed on the front end

For these reasons, the official Jupyter Server uses a binary-based WebSocket protocol. We could support exactly the same one, as an option, if needed:

https://jupyter-server.readthedocs.io/en/latest/developers/websocket-protocols.html

title: Support for connecting over IPC and/or domain socket instead of TCP
description:
Currently Kallichore only supports TCP as a transport. We should consider supporting other means of connecting to the server, for the following reasons:

- on servers, an open port that serves unsecured HTTP is often considered a security risk
- on desktops, a server process that listens on a local port can get blocked by a firewall (causing failures) or create end user prompts to allow the network traffic (causing confusion)
- local transports like domain sockets guarantee that no connections can be made from outside the host
- lower latency is possible

Relevant Rust crate:
https://docs.rs/hyperlocal/latest/hyperlocal/

title: Compile binary for all Linux platforms
description:
Currently, the Kallichore binary is not compiled with any special consideration for Linux, and consequently is not likely to work outside of the Linux version under which it is compiled in CI.

We should take a page out of Ark's playbook and use something like zig to avoid wrestling with glibc. 

https://github.com/posit-dev/ark/pull/486

We also want to avoid linking to OpenSSL if we can, which may be tricky since we use an HTTP library that supports SSL.

title: Validate bearer token when creating websocket connection
description:
Currently, Kallichore does bearer token validation on all the RPC endpoints that change state. For security reasons, we should also validate the bearer token when establishing a websocket connection; this is just a little more fiddly for the websocket endpoint since the Swagger crate doesn't extract the auth data from the request for us.

The token validation should go here:

https://github.com/posit-dev/kallichore/blob/e83476294cdd34bd2dc87117bbc1d6ed9cf6231a/crates/kcserver/src/server.rs#L694-L705

title: Shut down sessions gracefully on SIGINT/SIGCHLD
description:
Currently, terminating the Kallichore supervisor via `SIGINT` (when run in a terminal) or `SIGCHLD` (when e.g. run in Positron and Positron exits) results in the whole process tree getting taken down immediately. Any kernels are abruptly terminated without the chance to clean up.

We should trap these signals and give each running kernel a chance to shut down gracefully before Kallichore exits, by sending it a `shutdown_request`. Some period of grace should be provided to the kernel to clean up; then, Kallichore should forcefully exit any remaining kernels and exit itself.

title: Implement JEP 66: Use handshake to avoid socket allocation race condition
description:
JEP 66 proposes a method to avoid the classic Jupyter startup race condition, wherein some other process can take the ports in the period of time after the ports have been selected by the client but before ZeroMQ binds to them on the server side. 

https://jupyter.org/enhancement-proposals/66-jupyter-handshaking/jupyter-handshaking.html

Implemented on the Ark side here: https://github.com/posit-dev/ark/pull/576

title: Implement JEP 65: ensure IOPub messages are not missed by using XPUB
description:
Kallichore should implement JEP 65, which provides a way for clients to ensure IOPub messages are not missed due to a race condition.

JEP 65 is documented here: https://jupyter.org/enhancement-proposals/65-jupyter-xpub/jupyter-xpub.html

The corresponding work on the Ark side has already been merged: https://github.com/posit-dev/ark/pull/577
